claims.statement: Wilma Pearl Mankiller was born on November 18, 1945, in Tahlequah, Oklahoma, the capital of the Cherokee Nation, the sixth of eleven children; her father was a full-blood Cherokee. A Cherokee Nation release gave her birthplace as the W.W. Hastings Indian Hospital in Tahlequah; the Oklahoma Hall of Fame says she was born at Rock Mountain in Adair County.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors the true birth date and her Cherokee identity. The birthplace differs between sources; Tahlequah is used.

claims.statement: In 1979 she was nearly killed in a head-on car crash on a curve, in which the driver of the other car, one of her best friends, died. She needed about 17 operations; accounts say her leg was barely saved from amputation and that she was told she might never walk again. The Oklahoma Hall of Fame dates the crash to 1978 and describes shattered legs, broken ribs and a crushed face.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: New generalized myasthenia gravis in a 34-year-old Cherokee woman recovering from major trauma, on the 2016 and 2020 international consensus guidance for MG and the KDIGO 2025 ADPKD guideline. Drooping eyelids, double vision and fatigable weakness lead to the ice pack test, acetylcholine receptor antibodies (with MuSK held in reserve), repetitive nerve stimulation (with single-fiber EMG held in reserve), chest CT for thymoma, TSH, and forced vital capacity and negative inspiratory force, with the warning signs of myasthenic crisis. Treatment covers pyridostigmine, prednisone started low and raised slowly, azathioprine as a steroid-sparing agent after TPMT and infection screening, vaccination before immunosuppression, early thymectomy under the MGTX evidence, the place of newer targeted therapies such as efgartigimod and eculizumab, and the medicines to avoid in myasthenia gravis. Her documented hereditary polycystic kidney disease adds eGFR, urine albumin, kidney ultrasound with total kidney volume and the Mayo Imaging Classification, home blood pressure, water intake and avoiding NSAIDs. Care is culturally safe, with laboratory work through Cherokee Nation Health Services near her home and her own Cherokee medicine respected. Her documented diagnosis of myasthenia gravis less than a year after the 1979 crash, and her recovery with the help of Cherokee medicine people, surgery and drug therapy, frame the episode.

hpi.narrative: Ms. Mankiller returns two weeks after her first visit. On pyridostigmine 30 mg three times daily her eyelids lift for two to three hours after each dose, but double vision returns by evening and her arms still tire when she brushes her hair; she has mild stomach cramps and looser stools after doses. She has had no breathlessness, choking or weak cough. The acetylcholine receptor antibody test is strongly positive. The chest CT and kidney ultrasound were done last week. This morning she saw Dr. Okafor-Delaney of neuromuscular neurology, whose nerve stimulation test showed the typical decrement, and they agreed a plan: a higher pyridostigmine dose, prednisone started low and raised slowly, azathioprine once the screening tests are back, and an assessment for thymectomy. She asked that her blood tests be drawn near home where possible, and wants to understand each medicine before she takes it. She says the polycystic kidney disease is not new to her.

assessment.assessment: The diagnosis is confirmed by a positive antibody and a reproducible decrement on nerve stimulation; MuSK antibodies and single-fiber EMG are not needed. The weakness is mild to moderate and mainly ocular and limb, with mild bulbar involvement. Breathing measurements are normal, and there is no sign of impending crisis

Pyridostigmine alone is unlikely to control generalized disease. Prednisone is the first immunotherapy; starting at 10 mg and raising it by 10 mg a week to 40 mg lowers the risk of the early worsening that high starting doses can cause. A steroid-sparing agent is advised from the start because she is likely to need treatment for years. Azathioprine suits a woman of childbearing age better than mycophenolate, which must be avoided in pregnancy; it needs TPMT activity first, hepatitis B and tuberculosis screening, and regular blood counts and liver tests. Polycystic kidney disease with normal function does not change these doses. Pneumococcal and recombinant zoster vaccines should be given before immunosuppression, and live vaccines avoided

In non-thymomatous AChR antibody-positive generalized MG between 18 and 50, thymectomy early in the disease improves outcomes and lowers immunotherapy needs (MGTX). It is elective and should be done once she is stable. Her healed rib fractures do not prevent a robotic approach from the right; she should see thoracic surgery in about four weeks, with surgery once prednisone has taken effect, about two to three months from now

Efgartigimod, an FcRn blocker, and the complement inhibitors eculizumab and ravulizumab work well in AChR antibody-positive generalized MG, but the guidance places complement inhibitors after other immunotherapies have failed, and her disease is not refractory. They are kept in reserve. A complement inhibitor would need meningococcal vaccination first

assessment.display: Safety, medicines to avoid and kidney considerations
assessment.assessment: Fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, macrolides, telithromycin, magnesium by vein, beta-blockers and neuromuscular blocking drugs can worsen MG; statins and iodinated contrast need caution. Her kidney function is normal, so drug doses and contrast are not limited by it, but NSAIDs should be avoided for her kidneys and a beta-blocker should not be chosen if her blood pressure ever needs treatment
